seo.title: Antarctic Circle Fly-Cruise: 10 Days, No Drake Crossing
seo.description: Fly over the Drake Passage to King George Island, then sail the Antarctic Peninsula south to the Antarctic Circle at 66°33′S. 10 days from Punta Arenas, February 2027 and 2028, from US$24,995 pp.

answer: The Polar Circle Air-Cruise is a ten-day Antarctic voyage from Punta Arenas, Chile, that flies over the Drake Passage instead of sailing it: about two hours by charter to King George Island, then eight days aboard Magellan Explorer or Magellan Discoverer, two 88-guest expedition ships, south along the Antarctic Peninsula through the Gerlache and Penola straits and Crystal Sound to attempt the Antarctic Circle at 66°33′S, ice and weather permitting. It runs in February only, from US$24,995 per person.
quote: "I've stood on the Peninsula in March light. This is the voyage that goes past where I turned around."

map_title: Over the Drake and South to 66°33′S
suits: Two hours in the air instead of two days at sea, each way.
The Drake Passage is the roughest crossing on most Antarctic voyages. Flying it gives back four days and the seasickness that can come with them.
You've seen the Peninsula. Now go past where the classic route turns.
Most Peninsula voyages turn around near the Lemaire Channel. This one keeps going south through Crystal Sound to attempt the Circle.
Late-season light, low sun, and ice the size of towns.
February brings long golden evenings, calving glaciers and tabular icebergs. Possible, never guaranteed: whales feeding along the Peninsula.
An 88-guest ship, a balcony and nobody else on the horizon.
Small enough that the expedition team knows your name by the second day.
twice: The flights go when the weather allows.
Build a day or two of slack after the voyage; the operator's contingency plan covers the wait, not your onward flights.
The ice has the last word.
The voyage attempts 66°33′S. If the ice says no, the expedition team makes the most of every mile it can reach.
dayintro: The outline the ship sails south. In Antarctica the ice, wind and swell set the order day by day, and the expedition team chooses each landing on the morning. Open a day for the detail.

days.title: Punta Arenas
days.body: Arrive in Punta Arenas, on the Strait of Magellan, and transfer to your hotel. The mandatory pre-departure briefing is in the early afternoon at Antarctica21's Explorers House, so plan to land in the morning: it covers the flight, the landings and Antarctica's biosecurity rules. A welcome dinner follows that evening.
days.stay: Hotel in Punta Arenas [hotel to confirm per departure]

days.title: Fly to King George Island
days.line: Over the Drake, not through it
days.body: A charter flight of about two hours carries you over the Drake Passage to King George Island in the South Shetlands, landing near Chile's Frei Station and Russia's Bellingshausen Station. From the shore, Zodiacs take you out to the ship, and you sail the same afternoon. The flight goes only when the weather on the island allows it; the operator's contingency plan covers any wait in Punta Arenas.
days.stay: Aboard · Magellan Explorer or Magellan Discoverer
days.acts: Charter flight · Zodiac to the ship

days.title: The South Shetland Islands
days.body: The first full day in Antarctica, among the South Shetland Islands. The expedition team chooses the landings and Zodiac cruises on the day, by wind, swell and ice. Penguin colonies, fur and elephant seals and whalebone beaches are all possible here, never guaranteed.

days.title: The Gerlache Strait
days.body: Across the Bransfield Strait to the western side of the Antarctic Peninsula, and into the Gerlache Strait: steep mountains, tidewater glaciers and sheltered bays for landings and Zodiac cruising. Humpback whales are often seen feeding in these waters late in the season; possible, never guaranteed.

days.title: The Lemaire Channel and Penola Strait
days.body: If the ice lets the ship through, south by the Lemaire Channel and into the Penola Strait. This is the stretch where the classic Peninsula voyages usually turn around. On this voyage, the ship keeps going.

days.title: Crystal Sound and the Antarctic Circle
days.body: South into Crystal Sound and the attempt on the Antarctic Circle at 66°33′S. Whether the ship crosses it is decided on the day by the captain and the expedition leader, by sea ice and weather. The farther south you go, the more chance of Adélie penguins and of seals hauled out on the floes; possible, never guaranteed.

days.title: Northbound along the Peninsula
days.line: More landings on the way back
days.body: Northbound along the western Peninsula, with more landings, Zodiac cruises and, for those who booked it, sea kayaking. The expedition team uses the days on the way back to reach whatever the ice closed on the way down.

days.title: Back to the South Shetlands
days.body: Back north to the South Shetland Islands and King George Island, with a last landing or Zodiac cruise if conditions allow, and the farewell dinner aboard.

days.title: Fly to Punta Arenas
days.body: Zodiacs back to shore and the charter flight north to Punta Arenas, about two hours, weather permitting. Transfer to your hotel for the night.
days.stay: Hotel in Punta Arenas [hotel to confirm per departure]

days.title: Departure
days.body: Transfer to the airport for your flight home. Patagonia is on the doorstep: Torres del Paine is a few hours north by road, and we can add it before or after the voyage.

exp_title: On the ice, on the water and ashore

experiences.name: Crossing the Antarctic Circle
experiences.body: The reason this voyage exists. Beyond Crystal Sound, the ship tries for 66°33′S, the line south of which the sun doesn't set at midsummer. The captain and expedition leader decide on the day, by the ice.

experiences.name: Zodiac cruises among the ice
experiences.body: Small boats among the icebergs, brash ice and glacier faces, with an expedition guide at the tiller. The way to see the ice up close, and the way ashore.
experiences.james: The bergs look big from the deck. From a Zodiac, they look like architecture.

experiences.name: Shore landings
experiences.body: Guided landings on the islands and the Peninsula, chosen on the morning by the expedition team. Penguin colonies and seals are possible at many landings, never guaranteed. Waterproof boots are lent on board.

experiences.name: Sea kayaking
experiences.body: Guided sea kayaking in small groups when conditions allow, beneath sea cliffs and among the ice. Places are limited, so it's booked with the voyage.
experiences.james: I paddled under the cliffs on the Peninsula in 2020. It was the quietest I've ever heard the world.

experiences.name: Hiking and snowshoeing
experiences.body: Longer guided walks and snowshoe outings at selected landings, for those who want more than the standard landing.

experiences.name: The Polar Plunge and citizen science
experiences.body: The Polar Plunge into Antarctic water, for the brave, and citizen-science projects with the expedition team: the ship's contribution to what's known about these waters.

founder.title: Every Photograph Here Is His
founder.p1: James sailed the Antarctic Peninsula aboard HX's MS Roald Amundsen in February and March 2020, and was still there when the world shut down for COVID. Every photograph on this page outside the two Magellan ships is from that voyage: the Zodiacs among the bergs, the pink snow-algae landing, the kayaks under the cliffs, the postcard he wrote at Vernadsky Station.
founder.p2: He hasn't sailed this air-cruise or the two Magellan ships yet [confirm]. It's on file for the travellers who ask him the same two things about Antarctica: can I skip the Drake, and can I go further south than the usual voyage? This one does both.

firstTime.title: Why Fly In, and Why Go to the Circle
firstTime.intro: Antarctica is a long way to go to spend four days of it crossing the Drake. This voyage spends them on the ice.
points: The Drake Passage takes about two days each way by sea and can be rough. The charter flight takes about two hours.
Farther south than the classic route
Classic Peninsula voyages usually turn near the Lemaire Channel. This one carries on through Crystal Sound to try for 66°33′S.
February, the best month for it
Late in the season the sea ice is at its furthest south, the whales are feeding and the evening light is long and low.
88 guests at most, so everyone can be ashore at each landing within Antarctic visitor limits.
Hotel nights, transfers, the flights and the briefing are part of the fare. You only need to reach Punta Arenas.

faqs: Will I cross the Antarctic Circle?

The voyage attempts it, at 66°33′S in the waters beyond Crystal Sound. Sea ice and weather decide on the day, and the captain and expedition leader make the call. Sailing in February, when the ice has retreated furthest, gives the best chance; nobody can promise it.
Do I have to cross the Drake Passage by sea?
No. You fly over it: about two hours by charter from Punta Arenas to King George Island in the South Shetlands, and the same back. It saves roughly two days of open-ocean sailing each way.
What happens if the flight can't go?

The flights only go when the weather on King George Island allows a landing. The operator's flight contingency plan is part of the fare; delays of a day or more are possible either way, so leave room in your plans after the voyage.

From US$24,995 per person, double occupancy, aboard Magellan Explorer, and from US$29,795 aboard the newer Magellan Discoverer (fares on file for the 2027 and 2028 departures, to be confirmed when you enquire). The fare covers the charter flights, two hotel nights in Punta Arenas, all meals on board with wine and beer, landings, Zodiac cruises and lectures. Sea kayaking is extra.
February only: 5 and 13 February 2027, and 7 and 15 February 2028. It's the month when the sea ice has retreated far enough to sail south to the Circle.

Both carry 88 guests and were built for Antarctic air-cruises to the Polar Code. Magellan Discoverer is new for the 2026–27 season, with hybrid propulsion and a balcony in every cabin. Magellan Explorer, from 2019, has seven cabin categories and the lower fare. Tell us how you travel and we'll suggest the cabin.

Penguins, seals and whales are all likely somewhere on the voyage, but none is guaranteed: humpback whales feed along the Peninsula late in the season, and Adélie penguins and seals on the floes become more likely the farther south the ship gets. Possible, never guaranteed.
